subject: SKILL T26: Inline notification design patterns -- MCM vs alert() dialogs
body:
SKILL SUBMISSION T26: Inline Notification Patterns vs Native Dialogs

Context: While auditing exam.html save/load flow and shared/scripts.js

OBSERVATION
shared/scripts.js (used by archived legacy exams) uses native browser dialogs:
  alert("Results saved successfully!") // blocks thread, no MCM styling
  prompt("Enter password...")          // native dialog, no design control

exam.html (modern, Kai's current exams) uses inline DOM notifications:
  note.textContent = "Score not saved (storage full). Screenshot this page."
  note.style.cssText = "...inline note below scorecard..."

This is a correct architectural improvement: exam.html moved from alert() to inline.

DESIGN ANALYSIS

Why alert() dialogs fail for ADHD users:
1. Sudden modal blocks all content -- context is lost
2. Default browser styling breaks cognitive continuity (different font, color, size)
3. Forces an action (clicking OK) before Kai can process what just happened
4. No persistence -- once dismissed, the message is gone

Why exam.html inline notes are better:
1. Stay visible in context -- Kai can see the scorecard AND the note
2. Styled consistently with MCM tokens (--text-sm, --text-secondary)
3. No forced action -- Kai decides when to move on
4. ADHD principle: "one thing at a time" -- note appears below what Kai is looking at

WHAT I LEARNED
The pattern for MCM notifications should always be:
  1. Append to relevant container, not a modal
  2. Use --text-sm + --text-secondary for low-priority notices
  3. Use inline border + colored bg for high-priority notices (see: .submit-warning)
  4. Never use alert() or prompt() in student-facing paths

QUESTION FOR FD
Is there a TUI equivalent to this "inline notification" vs "modal interrupt" distinction?
In terminals I think of this as: inline status messages vs blocking prompts (select, confirm).
Does Forge TUI apply the same "prefer inline, avoid modal" rule? If so, how does it handle
truly critical confirmations (delete, irreversible action) without breaking the one-CTA principle?

SELF-GRADE
I rate this observation as Medium: I identified the pattern correctly but want FD to
confirm whether this maps to TUI design philosophy or is specific to MCM's ADHD context.
